cards.front: What is indicated by a dot placed above a single digit in a decimal?
cards.back: That digit repeats forever.

options.text: That digit repeats forever.
options.explanation: A dot above one digit marks that digit as recurring, so it continues indefinitely after the decimal point.

options.text: That digit appears only once.
options.explanation: A digit without recurring notation may appear only once. A dot above the digit instead indicates that it repeats forever.

options.text: That digit must be rounded up.
options.explanation: Rounding is determined by the digit to the right, not by a dot above a digit. The dot shows that the marked digit repeats forever.

options.text: That digit has a place value of zero.
options.explanation: The dot does not alter the digit’s place value or make it zero. It indicates that the marked digit repeats forever.

cards.front: How is a repeating block of digits (e.g. 0.3636...) shown using recurring notation?
cards.back: Dots are placed over the first and last digits of the repeating block.

options.text: Dots are placed over the first and last digits of the repeating block.
options.explanation: Marking the first and last digits identifies the boundaries of the entire repeating block, including every digit between the two dots.

options.text: Dots are placed over the first and second digits of the repeating block.
options.explanation: Using the first two digits does not show where a longer repeating block ends. Dots belong over the first and last digits of the block.

options.text: Dots are placed over the middle and last digits of the repeating block.
options.explanation: Starting the notation at a middle digit would omit part of the recurring block. The dots must mark its first and last digits.

options.text: Dots are placed over the last two digits of the repeating block.
options.explanation: Marking only the final two digits can falsely suggest that they alone recur. The first and last digits must be dotted to enclose the full block.

cards.front: In the notation $0.2\dot{4}\dot{9}$, only the digits [ ___ ] repeat.
cards.back: In the notation $0.2\dot{4}\dot{9}$, only the digits 4 and 9 repeat.

options.text: 4 and 9
options.explanation: The dots over 4 and 9 mark the beginning and end of the recurring block, so the block 49 repeats while 2 does not.

options.text: 2 and 4
options.explanation: The digit 2 appears before the first dot and is therefore non-recurring. The dotted boundaries show that 4 and 9 form the repeating block.

options.text: 2 and 9
options.explanation: The dot above 9 does not mean that 2 also recurs. The two dots enclose 4 and 9 as the complete repeating block.

options.text: 2, 4 and 9
options.explanation: Including 2 mistakes the whole decimal part for the recurring block. Only the digits from the first dotted digit to the last dotted digit repeat, namely 4 and 9.

cards.front: When converting a fraction using long division, how do you know the decimal will repeat?
cards.back: When the same remainder appears for a second time.

options.text: When the same remainder appears for a second time.
options.explanation: A repeated remainder causes the subsequent division steps and quotient digits to repeat in the same cycle, producing a recurring decimal.

options.text: When the same quotient digit appears for a second time.
options.explanation: A quotient digit can occur twice without beginning a repeating cycle. Repetition is guaranteed when the same remainder appears again, because the division process then repeats.

options.text: When a larger remainder appears for a second time.
options.explanation: The size of a remainder does not determine whether the decimal recurs. The decimal repeats when exactly the same remainder appears for a second time.

options.text: When a zero remainder appears for a second time.
options.explanation: A zero remainder makes the division terminate rather than recur. A recurring decimal is identified when the same non-zero remainder appears again.

cards.front: What is the core purpose of multiplying a recurring decimal by powers of 10 in algebra?
cards.back: To create two equations where the recurring tails are identical.

options.text: To create two equations where the recurring tails are identical.
options.explanation: Multiplying by a suitable power of 10 shifts complete recurring blocks so the infinite tails align and can be eliminated by subtraction.

options.text: To create two equations where the decimal points are identical.
options.explanation: Multiplying by 10 moves the decimal point rather than keeping it fixed. Its purpose is to make the recurring tails identical so subtraction removes them.

options.text: To create two equations where the whole-number parts are identical.
options.explanation: The whole-number parts normally become different after multiplication. The important feature is that the recurring tails become identical and therefore cancel under subtraction.

options.text: To create two equations where the recurring blocks are different.
options.explanation: Different recurring blocks would not cancel cleanly when the equations are subtracted. A suitable power of 10 is chosen to make the recurring tails identical.

cards.front: Why is subtraction used after lining up the recurring tails of two equations?
cards.back: To cancel out the infinite repeating part of the decimal.

options.text: To cancel out the infinite repeating part of the decimal.
options.explanation: Once the recurring tails are aligned, subtracting one equation from the other removes every repeated decimal digit, leaving a finite equation that can be solved.

options.text: To round off the infinite repeating part of the decimal.
options.explanation: The method gives an exact fraction and does not use rounding. Subtraction cancels the identical infinite repeating tails completely.

options.text: To double up the infinite repeating part of the decimal.
options.explanation: Adding the equations would combine rather than eliminate their recurring tails. Subtraction is used because identical tails cancel out exactly.

options.text: To shift left the infinite repeating part of the decimal.
options.explanation: Multiplication by a power of 10 shifts the decimal digits. Subtraction has the different purpose of cancelling the aligned infinite repeating part.

cards.front: Outline the algebraic steps to prove $0.\dot{6} = \frac{2}{3}$.
cards.back: Let $x = 0.666\dots$Multiply by 10 ($10x = 6.666\dots$)Subtract ($9x = 6$) and simplify $x = \frac{6}{9}$

options.text: Let $x = 0.666\dots$Multiply by 10 ($10x = 6.666\dots$)Subtract ($9x = 6$) and simplify $x = \frac{6}{9}$
options.explanation: Multiplying by 10 aligns the recurring tails. Subtracting the original equation gives $9x=6$, so $x=\frac{6}{9}=\frac{2}{3}$.

options.text: Let $x = 0.666\dots$Multiply by 10 ($10x = 6.666\dots$)Subtract ($9x = 6$) and simplify $x = \frac{6}{10}$
options.explanation: Dividing $9x=6$ by 10 is the slip; the coefficient of $x$ is 9. Dividing both sides by 9 gives $x=\frac{6}{9}=\frac{2}{3}$.

options.text: Let $x = 0.666\dots$Multiply by 10 ($10x = 6.666\dots$)Subtract ($10x = 6$) and simplify $x = \frac{6}{10}$
options.explanation: Subtracting $x$ from $10x$ gives $9x$, not $10x$. The correct equation is $9x=6$, which simplifies to $x=\frac{2}{3}$.

options.text: Let $x = 0.666\dots$Multiply by 10 ($10x = 6.666\dots$)Subtract ($-9x = -6$) and simplify $x = -\frac{6}{9}$
options.explanation: Dividing two negative quantities produces a positive result. From $-9x=-6$, the correct conclusion is $x=\frac{6}{9}=\frac{2}{3}$, not a negative fraction.

cards.front: What constitutes a fraction in its simplest form?
cards.back: The numerator and denominator have no common factors other than 1.

options.text: The numerator and denominator have no common factors other than 1.
options.explanation: A fraction is fully simplified when no integer greater than 1 divides both its numerator and denominator, so no further cancellation is possible.

options.text: The numerator and denominator have no common multiples other than 1.
options.explanation: Simplification depends on common factors, not common multiples; non-zero integers have many common multiples. The numerator and denominator must share no factor greater than 1.

options.text: The numerator and denominator are both prime numbers other than 1.
options.explanation: The numerator and denominator do not both need to be prime; for example, $8/15$ is simplified. They only need to have no common factor greater than 1.

options.text: The numerator and denominator have the same number of factors other than 1.
options.explanation: The number of factors each value has is irrelevant to simplification. A fraction is simplest when the numerator and denominator have no common factor greater than 1.

cards.front: To convert $0.3\dot{8}$ to a fraction, which two multiples of $x$ should be compared to align the tails?

options.explanation: There is one non-recurring digit and one recurring digit, so multiplying by 10 and 100 produces matching recurring tails that cancel when the equations are subtracted.
This comparison works when recurrence begins immediately after the decimal point. Here, the non-recurring 3 requires comparing $100x$ and $10x$ to align the recurring tails.
This shifts both decimals one place farther than necessary. Although the tails align, the standard minimal comparison is $100x$ and $10x$, based on one non-recurring and one recurring digit.
These multipliers differ by two decimal places, but the recurring block contains only one digit. Comparing $100x$ and $10x$ gives identical recurring tails for subtraction.

cards.front: To align tails for a decimal with $n$ non-recurring digits and a block of $r$ recurring digits, compare $\text{[...]}$ and $10^n x$.
cards.back: To align tails for a decimal with $n$ non-recurring digits and a block of $r$ recurring digits, compare $\boxed{10^{n+r}x}$ and $10^n x$.

options.explanation: Multiplying by $10^{n+r}$ shifts past both the $n$ non-recurring digits and one complete recurring block, allowing its tail to align with that of $10^n x$.
This accounts only for the recurring block and ignores the $n$ non-recurring digits. The required larger multiple is $10^{n+r}x$, which shifts past both sections.
Multiplying $n$ and $r$ is a common exponent error. The shifts for the non-recurring digits and recurring block are added, so the correct expression is $10^{n+r}x$.
Subtracting the block length reduces the shift rather than moving past both sections. Their lengths must be added, making the correct larger multiple $10^{n+r}x$.

cards.front: To align tails for a decimal with $n$ non-recurring digits and a block of $r$ recurring digits, compare $10^{n+r}x$ and $\text{[...]}$.
cards.back: To align tails for a decimal with $n$ non-recurring digits and a block of $r$ recurring digits, compare $10^{n+r}x$ and $\boxed{10^n x}$.

options.explanation: Multiplying by $10^n$ moves the non-recurring digits before the decimal point. Its recurring tail then aligns with the tail produced by multiplying by $10^{n+r}$.
This uses the recurring block length rather than the number of non-recurring digits. The smaller multiple must be $10^n x$ so that the recurring tails align.
Subtracting the recurring length from the non-recurring length does not identify the starting point of recurrence. The correct smaller multiple is $10^n x$.
The off-by-one exponent shifts too far unless the recurring block happens to have length one. The general smaller multiple is $10^n x$, determined only by the non-recurring digits.

cards.front: For the decimal $0.\dot{4}\dot{7}$, why is the decimal multiplied by 100 instead of 10?
cards.back: The repeating block has 2 digits; multiplying by 100 shifts the tail to match.

options.text: The repeating block has 2 digits; multiplying by 100 shifts the tail to match.
options.explanation: The block 47 contains two digits, so multiplication by $10^2=100$ moves one full block before the decimal point and leaves the same recurring tail.

options.text: The repeating block has 1 digit; multiplying by 100 shifts the tail to match.
options.explanation: Treating 47 as a one-digit block misreads the recurrence notation. Both 4 and 7 repeat, so the block has 2 digits and requires multiplication by 100.

options.text: The repeating block has 2 digits; multiplying by 10 shifts the tail to match.
options.explanation: Multiplication by 10 shifts only one digit, reversing the order of the recurring tail. A two-digit block requires multiplication by 100 to reproduce the same tail.

options.text: The repeating block has 100 digits; multiplying by 100 shifts the tail to match.
options.explanation: The multiplier does not equal the number of repeating digits. The block has 2 digits, and $100=10^2$ shifts exactly those two digits to align the tail.

cards.front: Is it necessary to separate the whole number (e.g., the 3 in $3.\dot{2}$) before using the algebra trick?
cards.back: No; let $x$ equal the entire decimal and use the standard method.

options.text: No; let $x$ equal the entire decimal and use the standard method.
options.explanation: The algebraic subtraction method works with the whole decimal, including its integer part. Setting $x=3.222\ldots$ and shifting the complete value still cancels the recurring tails correctly.

options.text: Yes; convert the whole number into a recurring decimal before using the standard method.
options.explanation: The integer part does not need to be rewritten as recurring. Let $x$ equal the entire decimal and apply the usual powers-of-ten multiplication and subtraction method directly.

options.text: Yes; remove the whole number and discard it before using the standard method.
options.explanation: Discarding the whole number changes the value and produces only the fractional part. The correct method lets $x$ equal the entire decimal, preserving both integer and recurring parts.

options.text: No; let $x$ equal only the recurring digit and use the standard method.
options.explanation: Setting $x$ equal only to a digit does not represent the original number. Instead, let $x$ equal the entire decimal and perform the standard shifting and subtraction steps.

cards.front: The final answer for a decimal greater than 1 (like $3.2\dot{6}\dot{3}$) is often an [ ___ ].
cards.back: The final answer for a decimal greater than 1 (like $3.2\dot{6}\dot{3}$) is often an improper fraction.

options.text: improper fraction
options.explanation: A decimal greater than 1 has a fractional representation whose numerator is larger than its denominator when written as a single fraction, so it is often an improper fraction.

options.text: proper fraction
options.explanation: A proper fraction is less than 1 because its numerator is smaller than its denominator. A decimal such as $3.2\dot{6}\dot{3}$ is greater than 1, so it gives an improper fraction.

options.text: unit fraction
options.explanation: A unit fraction has numerator 1 and is necessarily at most 1. A recurring decimal greater than 1 is instead commonly expressed as an improper fraction.

options.text: integer
options.explanation: A recurring decimal with a non-zero fractional part is not a whole number. When converted into one fraction, a value greater than 1 is generally an improper fraction.

cards.front: What is the resulting fraction for the recurring digit $a$ in the decimal $0.\dot{a}$?

options.explanation: If $x=0.aaa\ldots$, then $10x=a.aaa\ldots$. Subtracting gives $9x=a$, so $x=\frac{a}{9}$.
Dividing by 10 represents the terminating decimal $0.a$, not the recurring decimal $0.aaa\ldots$. Subtraction of $10x-x$ gives $9x=a$, so the fraction is $\frac{a}{9}$.
A denominator of 99 corresponds to a two-digit repeating block. Here only one digit repeats, so subtracting $x$ from $10x$ gives the correct result $\frac{a}{9}$.
This reverses the numerator and denominator after solving $9x=a$. Dividing both sides by 9 gives $x=\frac{a}{9}$, not its reciprocal.

cards.front: What is the resulting fraction for the repeating block in $0.\dot{0}\dot{a}$?

options.explanation: The repeating block is $0a$, which has two digits. If $x=0.0a0a\ldots$, then $100x=0a.0a\ldots$, giving $99x=a$ and therefore $x=\frac{a}{99}$.
A denominator of 9 applies to a one-digit repeating block. Here the repeating block is $0a$, so multiplying by 100 and subtracting gives $99x=a$ and $x=\frac{a}{99}$.
This would fit a non-recurring zero followed by recurring $a$, written with only $a$ recurring. Both 0 and $a$ are marked as recurring here, so the fraction is $\frac{a}{99}$.
A denominator of 100 represents the terminating decimal $0.0a$. Because the two-digit block $0a$ repeats indefinitely, subtraction produces a denominator of 99, giving $\frac{a}{99}$.

cards.front: How must recurring decimals be handled before performing multiplication or division?
cards.back: Convert every recurring decimal into a fraction first.

options.text: Convert every recurring decimal into a fraction first.
options.explanation: Fractions represent recurring decimals exactly, so multiplication or division can be completed without introducing rounding errors from an approximate decimal value.

options.text: Round every recurring decimal to a fixed number of places first.
options.explanation: Rounding replaces the recurring decimal with an approximation, which can make the final result inaccurate. Convert every recurring decimal into a fraction first to preserve its exact value.

options.text: Convert every recurring decimal into a percentage first.
options.explanation: Changing a recurring decimal into a percentage does not remove its recurring nature. It should be converted into an exact fraction before multiplication or division.

options.text: Treat every recurring decimal as a terminating decimal first.
options.explanation: A recurring decimal does not terminate, so cutting it off changes its value. Convert it into a fraction first so the calculation remains exact.

cards.front: When dividing fractions converted from recurring decimals, multiply by the [ ___ ] of the second fraction.
cards.back: When dividing fractions converted from recurring decimals, multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction.

options.text: reciprocal
options.explanation: Dividing by a fraction is equivalent to multiplying by its reciprocal, found by interchanging its numerator and denominator.

options.text: numerator
options.explanation: Using only the numerator ignores the denominator and changes the fraction’s value. Division requires multiplication by the reciprocal of the entire second fraction.

options.text: denominator
options.explanation: Using only the denominator is a common incomplete inversion error. The correct method is to swap both parts and multiply by the reciprocal.

options.text: additive inverse
options.explanation: The additive inverse changes a number’s sign and is used when dealing with subtraction. Fraction division instead requires the reciprocal of the second fraction.

cards.front: What distinguishes a terminating decimal from a recurring decimal?
cards.back: Terminating decimals stop after a fixed number of places.Recurring decimals have digits that repeat forever.

options.text: Terminating decimals stop after a fixed number of places.Recurring decimals have digits that repeat forever.
options.explanation: A terminating decimal has finitely many decimal places, whereas a recurring decimal contains a digit or block of digits that continues repeating indefinitely.

options.text: Terminating decimals repeat after a fixed number of places.Recurring decimals have digits that eventually stop.
options.explanation: These definitions have been reversed. Terminating decimals stop after finitely many places, while recurring decimals contain digits that repeat forever.

options.text: Terminating decimals stop after a fixed number of places.Recurring decimals have digits that repeat once.
options.explanation: The first statement is accurate, but recurring digits do not repeat only once. Their repeating pattern continues forever.

options.text: Terminating decimals continue after a fixed number of places.Recurring decimals have digits that repeat forever.
options.explanation: The second statement is accurate, but a terminating decimal does not continue indefinitely. It stops after a finite number of decimal places.

cards.front: Convert the fraction $\frac{7}{11}$ to recurring decimal notation.

options.explanation: Dividing 7 by 11 gives $0.636363\ldots$, so the repeating block is 63. Dots above 6 and 3 mark the beginning and end of that block.
This represents $0.363636\ldots$, which equals $\frac{4}{11}$. Dividing 7 by 11 instead produces the repeating block 63, giving $0.\dot{6}\dot{3}$.
This represents $0.63333\ldots$, where only 3 recurs. For $\frac{7}{11}$, both digits in the block 63 repeat, so both endpoints need dots.
This represents $0.707070\ldots$, not the result of dividing 7 by 11. Long division gives $0.636363\ldots$, written $0.\dot{6}\dot{3}$.

cards.front: Why is it a common mistake to compare $100x$ and $x$ for the decimal $0.3\dot{8}$?
cards.back: The recurring tails will not match (one starts at the first decimal place, the other at the second).

options.text: The recurring tails will not match (one starts at the first decimal place, the other at the second).
options.explanation: The multiplier should be chosen so the repeating sections begin in corresponding positions before subtraction. Here, the recurring 8 begins after the non-recurring 3 in $x$.

options.text: The recurring tails will match immediately (both start at the first decimal place).
options.explanation: In $x=0.3888\ldots$, the first decimal digit is the non-recurring 3, while after multiplying by 100 the recurring tail starts immediately. Their starting positions therefore differ.

options.text: Multiplying by 100 removes the recurring part (so $100x$ is a whole number).
options.explanation: Multiplication by 100 shifts the decimal point two places but does not remove an infinite recurring tail. The issue is that the recurring tails begin in different positions.

options.text: The non-recurring digit also repeats forever (so the entire decimal forms one recurring block).
options.explanation: Only the 8 repeats in $0.3\dot{8}$; the 3 occurs once. Consequently, the repeating tail begins at the second decimal place in $x$, not the first.
